newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Primakov arrives in Brussels for tough NATO talks.
newsitem.headline: Primakov arrives in Brussels for tough NATO talks.

text.p: Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov on Tuesday flew into Brussels for tough talks with NATO foreign ministers just hours after Moscow reiterated its opposition to the alliance's plans for eastward expansion.
Primakov, who did not talk to waiting reporters, was set to meet NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana and U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher later on Tuesday.
Before he left, Russian President Boris Yeltsin's press aide dismissed as "fantasy" suggestions Moscow was ready to accept NATO's eastward expansion plans.
"Russia's position on this issue remains firm and rather tough," Sergei Yastrzhembsky told a briefing earlier.

"It has not changed although our partners in dialogue have tried at various times to send to the world other signals... that Moscow has started to look more flexible, as if it had internally accepted such expansion. No. That is all fantasy."

NATO foreign ministers fixed a date for a summit next year to identify potential new members from central and eastern Europe -- former Kremlin Warsaw Pact allies -- a plan which Moscow says threatens its security.
The 16-member alliance insists it will not back down, but in a bid to reassure the Russians it has offered to negotiate a charter formalising relations between the two sides.

Defence officials say one possibility would be to form a new structure which might give Moscow a say in running the alliance. Russian contacts with NATO currently fall under the alliance's "16 plus one" structure, a body set up to hold talks between NATO and other countries.
"It is a little bit early to say what the method of consulation with Russia will be. We want to open a debate on this with our Russian friends," Solana told a news conference.
"May be on some issues it we could go a bit farther than 16 plus one," he added.
In another bid to calm tensions with Moscow, Christopher on Tuesday declared the alliance had no plans to station nuclear missiles on the territory of new members.
Russian officials have been united in fierce opposition to NATO's enlargement plans in recent weeks after several months of wavering between tough rejections and signs of compromise.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin voiced Russia's fears at a summit of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) in Lisbon last week, but most other leaders at the meeting backed NATO's plans.
"We think there are no arguments supporting NATO's eastward expansion," Yeltsin's press secretary, Yastrzhembsky said.

"It is a step which would lead only to negative consequences, above all for Russia and its national interests, and which to a certain degree would exclude Russia from this part of Europe and isolate Russia."
Despite his harsh comments, Yastrzhembsky said "new ideas" were starting to emerge from Western Europe and that they would be discussed in Brussels.
He gave no details but said: "In Lisbon (at the OSCE summit) we registered a certain change in the tone of the way the Russian arguments were taken."
